{{short description|Result about flat-foldable origami crease patterns}}
[[File:Kawasaki's theorem.jpg|thumb|280px|In this one-vertex crease pattern, the number of mountain folds (the five folds with the colored side out) differs by two from the number of valley folds (the three folds with the white side out)]]
'''Maekawa's theorem''' is a [[theorem]] in the [[mathematics of paper folding]] named after [[Jun Maekawa]]. It relates to flat-foldable [[origami]] [[crease pattern]]s and states that at every [[Vertex (geometry)|vertex]], the numbers of valley and mountain folds always differ by two in either direction.<ref>{{citation|last1=Kasahara|first1=K.|last2=Takahama|first2=T.|title=Origami for the Connoisseur|publisher=Japan Publications|location=New York|year=1987}}.</ref> The same result was also discovered by Jacques Justin<ref>{{citation|last=Justin|first=J.|title=Mathematics of origami, part 9|journal=British Origami|date=June 1986|pages=28–30}}.</ref> and, even earlier, by S. Murata.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Murata | first = S.
 | journal = Bulletin of Junior College of Art
 | language = Japanese
 | pages = 29–37
 | title = The theory of paper sculpture, II
 | volume = 5
 | year = 1966}}.</ref>

==Parity and coloring==
One consequence of Maekawa's theorem is that the total number of folds at each vertex must be an [[even number]]. This implies (via a form of [[Dual graph|planar graph duality]] between [[Eulerian graph]]s and [[bipartite graph]]s) that, for any flat-foldable crease pattern, it is always possible to [[graph coloring|color]] the regions between the creases with two colors, such that each crease separates regions of differing colors.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Hull | first = Thomas | authorlink = Tom Hull (mathematician)
 | contribution = On the mathematics of flat origamis
 | contribution-url = http://www.organicorigami.com/thrackle/class/hon394/papers/HullOldFlatFoldabilityPaper.pdf
 | mr = 1382321
 | pages = 215–224
 | series = Congressus Numerantium
 | title = Proceedings of the Twenty-Fifth Southeastern International Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing (Boca Raton, FL, 1994)
 | volume = 100
 | year = 1994}}. See in particular Theorem&nbsp;3.1 and Corollary&nbsp;3.2.</ref> The same result can also be seen by considering which side of the sheet of paper is uppermost in each region of the folded shape.

==Related results==
Maekawa's theorem does not completely characterize the flat-foldable vertices, because it only takes into account the numbers of folds of each type, and not their angles.
[[Kawasaki's theorem]] gives a complementary condition on the angles between the folds at a vertex (regardless of which folds are mountain folds and which are valley folds) that is also necessary for a vertex to be flat-foldable.
